title: Core-energy concentration in rotationally superposed apodized catastrophe fields
summary: Rotational superposition changes both the symmetry and the energy distribution of a structured optical field.
abstract: Rotational superposition changes both the symmetry and the energy distribution of a structured optical field. We study this redistribution for Gaussian-apodized Pearcey and butterfly fields in scalar free-space propagation. Decomposing a field into inversion-even and inversion-odd components shows that coherent addition to its 180◦ rotated copy selects the even component. The resulting change in power inside a circular observation region depends on the concentration of the two components, rather than on a new propagation law. We combine this description with equal-budget searches over a common bounded phase family. After fixing the selected parameters, the Pearcey and butterfly compositions reach median core-energy fractions of 5.965% and 5.901%, respectively, compared with 3.970% for the strongest Gaussian control with the same phase bounds and composition options. Mesh refinement, an expanded window, denser axial sampling, and direct Fresnel quadrature test the numerical observations. A separate frozen-field decomposition measures even-port throughputs of 91.84% and 93.32% for the two catastrophe sources and distinguishes normalized concentration from incident-power delivery. An ideal Gaussian thin-lens reference is reported separately because it exceeds the imposed quadratic-phase range. These results support a conditional concentration advantage within the stated field and phase classes; the advantage does not establish superiority over unrestricted focusing optics.
limitations: Simulation study. The advantage depends on the stated field and phase constraints. Peer review and prior-art novelty have not been established.

title: Limits of quadratic phase surrogates for finite-core collection in apodized beams
summary: A low-order phase approximation can preserve an input-plane statistic while changing the power collected after propagation.
abstract: A low-order phase approximation can preserve an input-plane statistic while changing the power collected after propagation. We test two quadratic surrogates for a radial quartic phase in Gaussian, Pearcey and butterfly fields: one matches the intensity-weighted mean phase, and the other minimizes the intensity-weighted squared phase-gradient error. Both coefficients are calculated before propagation without fitting output data. The observable is the median power fraction inside a fixed on-axis circular core over a free-space axial interval. Across three quartic coefficients, the first surrogate gives residual ratios of 0.81–0.89 relative to its own departure from the unmodified field. The Gaussian reference therefore fails the original proposed equivalence test. The phase-gradient surrogate also underestimates the quartic core fraction, by 9.51–23.27% across the primary cases. Complete-arm mesh, axial-grid and independent Fresnel checks distinguish a persistent surrogate discrepancy from circular-core discretization. The resulting comparisons characterize the limits of these two low-order reductions for the specified fields and collection geometry.
limitations: Numerical simulation study; see the manuscript for scope and unresolved tests.

title: Quadratic Chirp and Fixed-Axis Core Collection from a Finite-Energy Airy Beam
summary: A quadratic phase changes transverse phase gradients without changing the source-plane intensity.
abstract: A quadratic phase changes transverse phase gradients without changing the source-plane intensity. We numerically test the registered prediction that a chirp of amount c = −0.5 raises the median fraction of power inside a fixed on-axis circular core for a finite-energy Airy source with scale 0.20 mm and apodization 0.10, propagated in free space from 0.04 to 0.08 m. In the executed 384 × 384 angular-spectrum calculation, the transformed and base median core fractions are 0.072402 and 0.062833, respectively, giving a ratio of 1.1528. A 576 × 576 reference calculation gives the same ratio to four decimal places. Mesh, window, axial-sampling, and independent paraxial Fresnel checks give ratios near 1.153; the zero-chirp identity control is validated. A measured c = +0.5 comparison gives a ratio below unity, about 0.876, but is a secondary comparison and does not establish a general chirp-sign law. Centroid-aligned collection is higher than fixed-axis collection in both arms, so the primary endpoint reflects both position and intensity distribution. The result supports the registered numerical prediction for this source and collection geometry, but does not isolate a unique mechanism or establish a distinction from the broader literature on chirped Airy beams.
limitations: AI review: Weak reject; revision needed. Numerical simulation study; see the manuscript for scope and unresolved tests.

title: Fixed-axis core collection after a vortex-phase transformation of a Gaussian beam
summary: A phase-only transformation preserves an input beam’s intensity while changing the phase that governs its subsequent diffraction.
abstract: A phase-only transformation preserves an input beam’s intensity while changing the phase that governs its subsequent diffraction. We test a registered, condition-specific prediction: for a Gaussian beam with a 0.10 mm amplitude waist, applying a charge +2 vortex phase in free space gives a transformed-to-base ratio no greater than one for the median power fraction in a fixed on-axis circular core over z = 0.03–0.08 m. The 633 nm, 1 W fields are propagated without a lens, and the core radius is 0.10 mm. At the reference numerical tier, the transformed and base median core efficiencies are 0.01763695 and 0.59284526, respectively, giving a ratio of 0.02974967. The transformed core fraction is lower at all five sampled planes. A charge-zero identity control passes; mesh, window, axial-grid, wavelength, quantization, noise-probe, and independent-propagator checks reproduce the directional comparison across the tested variants. These results support the registered prediction for this scalar finite-core observable. They do not isolate a vortex-specific mechanism, establish a charge law or topology, or establish novelty.
limitations: AI review: Weak reject; revision needed. Numerical simulation study; see the manuscript for scope and unresolved tests.
